Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
You can never know who will harm you
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other endorsed items center on partner-violence-related threat monitoring, hypervigilance, sensory memory, and danger appraisals. In contrast, restrictive eating reflects a different coping theme that is not echoed elsewhere in Threat, Memory, or Negative Appraisals, and it sits awkwardly with the formulation in which Maladaptive Strategies feed Threat. Scanning surroundings and mirror checking plausibly amplify threat, but strict eating control does not connect clearly to the described trauma pattern.

vignette: Nina, a 48-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married tutor, has experienced profound distress since enduring physical abuse at the hands of her romantic partner. Her trauma symptoms have significantly impacted her daily life, causing her to constantly scan her environment for any signs of threat, check mirrors obsessively, and remain hyperalert towards potentially dangerous people. The traumatic event itself involved repeated instances of violence in their home, which Nina remembers vividly but fragmented. Each memory appears as disconnected pieces that do not fit together seamlessly, yet the terror she experienced during each incident comes flooding back with such intensity that it feels like reliving them through photographic recall. This fragmented nature of her memories fuels her constant fear and hypervigilance, reinforcing her belief that she has been permanently damaged by the experience. Nina's negative appraisals have further exacerbated her memory issues. She is certain that she will never be fully herself again and feels like an outsider in her own life. This sense of being forever changed for the worse deepens her fragmented memories and makes each recall more terrifying, as she relives the events with a heightened sense of dread. As a result, her memories of the abuse have become even more intrusive and distressing. Her hypervigilance extends beyond mere alertness; it has evolved into a constant scanning for potential threats, particularly weapons or dangerous objects in any environment she encounters. This hypervigilance is not just about noticing physical dangers but also involves reacting to perceived threats before her mind can process them fully. Her body's automatic response to danger compounds her fear that anyone could potentially harm her at any moment. Nina's daily life as a tutor has been profoundly affected by these symptoms. In the classroom, she constantly checks mirrors and scans the room for signs of potential threats, which distracts her from teaching effectively. This hypervigilance leads to increased anxiety during interactions with students and colleagues, making it challenging to maintain professional relationships. The fragmented pieces of her memories also influence her behavior outside work. For instance, while driving home, she frequently checks mirrors, ensuring no one is following or lurking nearby. At home, she remains vigilant for any signs that someone could harm her again. This constant state of alertness has led to a growing sense of isolation and fear. Nina's belief that she will never be the same person as before and her feeling of being an outsider now have become deeply entrenched in her daily life. She feels constantly on edge, and each memory triggers a cycle of heightened threat perception and maladaptive strategies. This loop has made it difficult for her to function normally in her personal and professional life. What finally brought Nina to seek help was the realization that her constant fear and hypervigilance were taking a toll not only on herself but also on her relationships with her family and colleagues. She is most afraid of never feeling safe again, yet she hopes that through therapy, she can regain some sense of normalcy and feel more in control of her life. Nina's current state reflects the intertwined nature of her negative appraisals, memory issues, threat perception, and maladaptive strategies. Each symptom feeds into the other, creating a cycle of distress and fear that has become increasingly difficult for her to manage on her own.
